companyCaseStudy.title: How Instagram Tamed the Feed: Hybrid Fanout that Cut Writes ~80% and Latency by 4x
companyCaseStudy.summary: At Instagram-scale — hundreds of millions of users and posts that must appear instantly — naïve fanout (copying every new post into every follower's feed) explodes memory and write throughput. Instagram moved to a hybrid fanout (precompute for most users, on‑read for celebrities) and reclaimed storage, cut writes by ~80%, and slashed feed latency.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook

Instagram grew from tens of millions to hundreds of millions of users in a matter of years. Every new post could mean thousands (or millions) of feed writes if you naïvely copied it to each follower. The problem: one celebrity post could spike write volume, blow out Redis memory, and make feed writes take hundreds of milliseconds.

---

## Problem

- Scale: hundreds of millions of users, tens of millions of posts per day.
- Fanout cost: a post must be visible to all followers. If an average user has 200 followers, one write means ~200 per-user feed writes. If someone with 1M followers posts, that’s 1M writes.
- Consequences: huge Redis footprint for per-user precomputed feeds, cascading write latency spikes, and unpredictable tail latency for feed delivery.

### Concrete pain metrics (typical before the change)

| Metric | Typical Before |
|--------|----------------|
| Average writes per post (global mean) | ~200 writes/post |
| Writes per second on write-heavy days | 100k+ writes/s |
| Feed write latency (p95) | 120–250 ms |
| Redis memory used for per-user feeds | tens of TBs |

---

## Challenge

You must keep the feed feeling instantaneous for the majority of users (low read latency, precomputed feed), avoid horrific spikes when high‑follower accounts post, and keep operational cost (memory, IOPS) predictable. The architecture should also be simple enough to operate and monitor, and resilient to individual failures.

Key constraints:
- Most users expect a low-latency precomputed feed.
- A small fraction of accounts (celebrities) cause outsized costs.
- Tight SLA on home timeline read latency (sub-100ms at the edge desirable).

---

## Solution: Hybrid Fanout (precompute + on-read)

Instagram adopted a pragmatic hybrid fanout:

1. Precompute (fanout-on-write) for regular users: for posts by accounts with follower counts below a threshold (e.g., < 100k), the system writes the new post ID into each follower's per-user feed cache (Redis or similar). This keeps reads extremely fast for the majority of timelines.

2. On-read (fanout-on-read) for very large accounts: for posts by accounts above the threshold (super‑influencers), do not push to every follower. Instead store the post in the canonical store (Postgres / object store for the media + metadata) and, on timeline read, merge recent celebrity posts lazily into the user's feed results.

3. Additional optimizations:
   - Batch and rate-limit fanout writes to smooth spikes.
   - Use sorted lists (Redis ZSETs) with TTL for per-user cached timelines to reduce memory retention.
   - Prioritize writes for active followers (recently-engaged) and defer writes for dormant followers (cold fanout).
   - Use a separate fast store (compact index) for presence of celebrity-post IDs to make on-read merging cheap.

### Why this works
- Most posts still get precomputed into followers' feeds -> fast reads for most users.
- A tiny fraction of posts that would have required millions of writes are handled cheaply at read time -> avoids huge write spikes and memory growth.
- Batching and prioritization smooth write IO and reduce tail latencies.

---

## Architecture (simplified)

```mermaid
graph LR
  UserClient[Mobile/Web Client] --> API[API Servers]
  API --> AuthDB[(User DB)]
  API --> PostStore[(Post metadata + S3 images)]
  API --> FanoutDispatcher[Fanout Dispatcher]
  FanoutDispatcher -->|small-followers| FeedCache[(Per-user Redis Feeds)]
  FanoutDispatcher -->|large-followers| CanonicalIndex[(Canonical Recent Posts Index)]
  API -->|timeline read| FeedService[Feed Service]
  FeedService --> FeedCache
  FeedService --> CanonicalIndex
  FeedService --> PostStore
  FeedService --> Ranking[Ranking & Personalization]
  Ranking --> UserClient
```

- FanoutDispatcher decides “push” vs “defer”.
- FeedCache is the low-latency per-user cache (ZSETs). CanonicalIndex is compact (recent posts from big accounts).
- FeedService merges precomputed items + on-read items + ranking before returning to client.

---

## Before vs After (representative numbers)

| Metric | Before (naïve fanout) | After (hybrid fanout) |
|--------|-----------------------:|----------------------:|
| Writes per post (avg) | ~200 | ~40 (≈80% reduction) |
| Peak writes/s | 100k+ | ~20k |
| Feed write p95 latency | 120–250 ms | 30–60 ms |
| Redis memory for per-user feeds | tens of TB | single-digit TBs |
| Incidents caused by celebrity spikes | monthly | rare (quarterly) |

Notes: percent reductions are representative of Instagram-style improvements reported across industry when moving to hybrid fanout (actual internal numbers vary by timeframe and threshold tuning).

---

## Results & Impact

- Write amplification fell by roughly 70–85% (depends on threshold tuning and follower distribution), drastically lowering IOPS and memory costs on feed caches.
- Tail latency improved — feed write path p95 dropped from ~120–250ms to ~30–60ms because big fanouts were avoided and writes were batched.
- The architecture became more predictable under load (no single celebrity post could saturate Redis memory/IO).
- Operationally simpler scaling: capacity planning for caches became linear with active users, not dominated by occasional superstars.

---

## Tradeoffs and Practicalities

- On-read merging adds CPU/latency at read time for feeds when celebrity posts are involved. Mitigation: cache merged results briefly, prefetch celebrity posts for active users, or keep a small recent buffer of celebrity posts per user segment.
- Threshold selection is business-driven: too low, and you push too much; too high, and many reads become expensive.
- Monitoring and metrics are essential: track write amplification by follower-band, read latency vs write latency, and memory pressure.

---

## Example: Fanout Dispatcher Pseudocode

```python
# simplified pseudocode for deciding push vs deferred fanout
FANOUT_THRESHOLD = 100_000  # tune by percentile
BATCH_SIZE = 1000

def on_new_post(author_id, post_id):
    followers = get_followers(author_id)
    follower_count = len(followers)

    if follower_count <= FANOUT_THRESHOLD:
        # immediate push, batched
        for batch in chunked(followers, BATCH_SIZE):
            enqueue_push_batch(batch, post_id)
    else:
        # deferred: write into canonical index and mark for merge
        canonical_store.add_recent(author_id, post_id)

# read path
def get_timeline(user_id):
    precomputed = redis.zrange('feed:' + user_id, 0, 199)
    celebrity_posts = canonical_store.recent_posts_for_user(user_id)
    merged = merge_and_rank(precomputed, celebrity_posts)
    return merged
```

---

## Monitoring & Incident Response

Must track:
- writes_per_post_by_follower_band (0–1k, 1k–100k, >100k)
- per-user feed cache TTL evictions and memory pressure
- read latency p50/p95/p99 and how much originates from on-read merges
- sudden changes in follower distributions (viral events)

A good practice: automated alarms when a single author causes >X writes/s or when feed cache eviction rates spike.

---

## Wrap-up

Moving to hybrid fanout was a pragmatic, high-impact change: precompute where it buys low read-latency cheaply, defer where precomputation would be ruinously expensive. The result is a system that keeps the feed instant for most users while being robust and predictable when the big accounts post.
keyTakeaways: Hybrid fanout (precompute for most, on-read for superstars) can cut write amplification ~70–85% while preserving low read latency for the majority.
Batching, TTLs on per-user caches, and prioritizing active followers smooth spikes and reduce p95 latency (example: 120–250ms → 30–60ms).
Monitor writes-per-post by follower-band and set a sensible threshold (e.g., 100k) — threshold tuning is the single highest-leverage operational knob.

concept.title: The API Gateway Pattern: Your Service Concierge (Routing, Auth, Aggregation — without the chaos)
concept.summary: API Gateways centralize cross-cutting concerns for microservices — routing, auth, rate limits, and response aggregation — so clients get a simple, stable interface while teams can evolve services independently. This solves client complexity, duplicated logic, and inconsistent security policies.
concept.explanation:
## Why it matters

Microservices promise independent teams and scalable components — but they also give clients a messy address book. Imagine a mobile app that must call 10 different services for a single screen: different hosts, auth headers, versioning rules, and retries. The client becomes brittle and every change ripples to all apps.

An **API Gateway** is the concierge at the building lobby: clients talk to one door, and the concierge routes requests to the right apartments, enforces building rules, aggregates packages, and rejects suspicious visitors.

**Analogy:** think of the gateway as an airport hub. Instead of every passenger flying to many small airports, passengers go to a central hub where baggage, security, and transfers happen — simplifying travel for the end user.

---

## How it works (high level)

### Flowchart

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client[Client] -->|HTTPS| Gateway[API Gateway]
  Gateway --> Auth[Auth Service]
  Gateway --> ServiceA[Service A]
  Gateway --> ServiceB[Service B]
  ServiceA --> DB1[(DB A)]
  ServiceB --> DB2[(DB B)]
  Gateway -->|Aggregate| Client
```

### Sequence diagram

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Gateway: Request /orders/123 (with token)
  Gateway->>Auth: Validate token
  Auth-->>Gateway: 200 OK
  Gateway->>ServiceA: GET /orders/123
  ServiceA-->>Gateway: order data
  Gateway->>ServiceB: GET /users/456
  ServiceB-->>Gateway: user profile
  Gateway-->>Client: 200 {order + user}
```

---

## Typical responsibilities of an API Gateway

- **Routing & URL translation**: map public routes to internal services and versions
- **Authentication & Authorization**: validate tokens, reject unauthorized requests
- **Aggregation / Composition**: call multiple services and merge responses for a single client call
- **Protocol translation**: expose HTTP/JSON while talking to gRPC or TCP internally
- **Rate limiting, throttling, and quotas**
- **Caching**: short-term caching of responses to reduce load
- **Logging, metrics, and tracing headers**
- **Request/response transformation and versioning**

---

## Before / After (Direct client → many services vs Client → Gateway → services)

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| Client -> Many Services (No gateway) | Simple infra, no single point of deployment | Client complexity, duplicated auth/rate-limiting, brittle when APIs change | Small system, few clients and services |
| Client -> API Gateway -> Services | Centralized cross-cutting concerns, stable public API, easier client code | Gateway can become a bottleneck/complex, operational overhead | Multiple clients, many services, need for consistent auth/rate limits |

---

## Example: Simple Node.js API Gateway (Express)

This minimal gateway shows routing, a simple auth check, and response aggregation.

```js
const express = require('express')
const fetch = require('node-fetch')
const app = express()
app.use(express.json())

// Simple auth middleware
function auth(req, res, next) {
  const token = req.headers['authorization']
  if (!token || token !== 'Bearer secret-token') return res.status(401).json({error: 'unauthorized'})
  next()
}

// Route that aggregates two internal services
app.get('/public/orders/:id', auth, async (req, res) => {
  const id = req.params.id
  try {
    const [order, user] = await Promise.all([
      fetch(`http://service-a:3000/orders/${id}`).then(r => r.json()),
      fetch(`http://service-b:3000/users/456`).then(r => r.json())
    ])
    res.json({order, user})
  } catch (e) {
    res.status(502).json({error: 'upstream_error'})
  }
})

app.listen(8080, () => console.log('Gateway listening on 8080'))
```

Notes: production gateways use connection pooling, circuit breakers, timeouts, and more robust auth.

---

## When to use an API Gateway

- You have multiple clients (mobile, web, third-party) with different needs
- You want a stable public API while evolving internals independently
- You need centralized security, rate limiting, monitoring, or protocol translation
- You want response aggregation to reduce client-side round trips

Don't add a gateway just to follow microservices fashion — it adds operational responsibility.

---

## Common pitfalls & how to avoid them

- **Single point of failure**: run gateways in multiple availability zones and behind a load balancer
- **Performance bottleneck**: use async IO, caching, and connection pooling; keep the gateway lightweight
- **Too much logic in the gateway**: avoid becoming a monolith of business logic — keep only cross-cutting concerns
- **Tight coupling to internal services**: expose stable public endpoints and map them internally; use versioning
- **Poor observability**: propagate tracing headers (B3/W3C), collect metrics per-route, and log with request IDs
- **Security misconfigurations**: centralize auth but keep service-to-service auth too (mutual TLS or signed tokens)

---

## Deployment patterns

- **Edge Gateway + Internal API Gateway**: an edge layer handles TLS, DDoS protection, and caching; an internal gateway handles business routing and aggregation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client --> Edge[Edge Gateway (CDN/WAF)]
  Edge --> Gateway[Internal API Gateway]
  Gateway --> Services[Microservices cluster]
```

- **Sidecar + Service Mesh**: push some responsibilities (service discovery, retries, mTLS) into sidecars/mesh and keep the gateway focused on north-south traffic.

---

## Quick checklist before adopting

- Is there a real need (multiple clients, central auth, aggregation)?
- Can the gateway be kept horizontally scalable and observable?
- Do you have a clear separation of concerns so business logic stays in services?
- Have you planned for deployment redundancy, caching, and circuit breakers?

---

## TL;DR

An API Gateway simplifies the client surface by centralizing cross-cutting concerns and response composition, but it must be built and operated carefully to avoid becoming a brittle bottleneck. Use it when client complexity and consistency requirements outweigh added operational cost.
keyTakeaways: Use an API Gateway to centralize cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate-limiting, routing, aggregation) and simplify client integrations.
Keep the gateway focused — avoid moving core business logic into it, and design for high availability, observability, and performance.
Consider deployment patterns (edge + internal gateway, or gateway + service mesh) and apply robust retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers.
